title: California's First Diwali Under a Partly Struck-Down Holiday Law
excerpt: AB 268 made Diwali a state holiday from January 1, but a court struck down parts of it in July. With Diwali falling on Sunday, November 8 this year, celebrations are unaffected — the open questions land next year.
body:
• California's Diwali holiday law, AB 268, took effect on January 1, 2026, making the state the third in the US to officially recognise Diwali.
  • In July 2026, a court struck down parts of the law; the Hindu American Foundation said the ruling targeted the law's wording about Diwali's religious significance, and the full court order had not been released in the reports.
  • The law never created a mandatory paid holiday: it let eligible state employees use paid leave for Diwali and allowed public schools and community colleges to close.
  • This year Diwali falls on Sunday, November 8, 2026, so the school and work question is moot for most Californians — but check your own employer or district policy before assuming any leave entitlement.

California celebrates Diwali this Sunday, November 8, under a state holiday law that a court has already partly struck down. The sequence matters for the hundreds of thousands of Hindu, Jain, Sikh and Buddhist Californians who welcomed the law last year: the recognition is on the books, parts of it have been invalidated, and exactly which parts remains unclear in the reporting so far.

What the law did

Assembly Bill 268, introduced by Assemblymember Ash Kalra and signed by Governor Gavin Newsom on October 6, 2025, designated Diwali as a California state holiday and took effect on January 1, 2026. California became the third US state to officially recognise Diwali, after Pennsylvania and Connecticut.

The law was narrower than the headline suggested. It did not create a mandatory paid holiday for everyone. Eligible state employees could take a paid day off to observe the festival, public schools and community colleges were permitted to close on Diwali, and schools were authorised to hold educational activities marking its cultural importance. Diwali was expressly not made a judicial holiday, so courts stay open.

What the court did

In July 2026, less than a year after the law took effect, a Sacramento County Superior Court judge ruled in favour of the San Francisco Taxpayers Association, which had petitioned against the law arguing it was too costly — it estimated closures and paid leave could cost taxpayers as much as $68.8 million, according to court documents reported by Fresnoland — and that it gave preferential treatment to a religious holiday in violation of the US and California constitutions. July coverage described the ruling as striking down parts of the law, according to the Hindu American Foundation (HAF), which said it is monitoring the case. The foundation said the ruling focused on the wording of the law describing Diwali's religious significance, rather than its practical purpose of letting students and employees observe the festival without choosing between their faith and their school or work responsibilities. Reporting at the time noted that the court order itself had not been released and that it was not clear whether the law had been overturned entirely or in parts.

"The ruling focused on the wording of the law describing Diwali's religious significance, rather than the practical purpose of the holiday: allowing students and employees to observe an important festival without being forced to choose between their faith and their educational or professional responsibilities."

— Hindu American Foundation

HinduPACT, another Hindu American advocacy group, called the decision a setback. "For Hindu families, the ruling is more than a legal setback. It threatens a hard-won measure of equal recognition and sends a painful message to a community that has long sought the same dignity and accommodation afforded to other faith traditions," the group said. Its founder and chair, Ajay Shah, said he would work with community leaders, legal experts and lawmakers to help restore the protections.

What it means this Diwali

Two things soften the ruling's practical impact this year. First, Diwali falls on a Sunday, so schools are closed and most state offices are shut regardless of the law's status. Second, the California Assembly separately adopted House Resolution 137, introduced by Assembly Members Patel and Kalra, which recognises this year's Diwali festival on Sunday, November 8, 2026, and encourages Californians to take part in the celebration.

The open questions land next year, when Diwali falls on a weekday again: whether state employees retain the paid-leave option the law created, and whether districts that planned Diwali closures can still schedule them, depends on the final shape of the court case and any legislative fix. HAF says it "will continue supporting Hindu Americans in California as we work to protect the ability of our community to celebrate the holidays that matter." For this weekend, the practical advice is simple: celebrations are unaffected, and anyone relying on a Diwali leave entitlement should confirm it with their employer or school district rather than assume the 2026 law still applies in full.
